units.title: Filter the Clarity dashboard to a roughly six-month sample period

claim.text: The source says the first thing it does on the main Clarity dashboard is filter for a good enough sample size or sample period.
claim.quote: filter for a good enough sample size or good enough sample period

action.text: Set the dashboard date range to roughly the last 6 months, or the last 90 days when less history exists.
action.quote: typically that's going to be the last 6 months of data it could also be last 90 days of data

args.text: Opening the main Clarity dashboard to review metrics.
args.quote: the first thing that I like to do when looking at the main dashboard

args.text: Clarity must have been set up long enough ago to retain the desired window; the source says this varies by account.
args.quote: depending on when you set up Clarity you may or may not have the ability to go that far back

completion.text: The window selected is roughly six months; the exact boundary does not have to match.
completion.quote: so roughly 6 months doesn't have to be exact

unknowns: The source calls 6 months generally good while also offering last 90 days, without a rule for choosing between them.

units.title: Prioritize the Insights block over baseline KPIs on the main dashboard

claim.text: The source identifies the Insights block as the part of the main dashboard that is important to focus on.
claim.quote: the part that I find is important to focus on on the main dashboard is really this insights block here

args.text: Most other dashboard metrics can be pulled from Google Analytics and are not unique to Clarity.
args.quote: a lot of the metrics on the main Clarity dashboard you can actually pull directly from Google analytics

unknowns: The named baseline KPIs (scroll depth, active time, pages per session, total sessions) are described as obtainable elsewhere, not as unusable.

units.title: Open recordings from an insight metric's camera icon and watch them

claim.text: The source says watching the matching recordings is worthwhile when a rage-click metric warrants a particular change, to see where people hit frustration or friction.
claim.quote: if the rage clicks actually warrant particular change then it's worth watching those recordings to see you know where people experiencing frustration or friction

action.text: Click the camera icon next to the insight metric to open the recordings page and watch the sessions of people who experienced that insight.
action.quote: you can actually click on this little camera icon and it's going to open up the recordings page where you can watch the actual recordings of people that experienced the rage clicks

args.text: A rage-click rate is displayed in the dashboard Insights block.
args.quote: rage clicks is the first one here which sits at 0 2%

unknowns: The source's fuller recordings walkthrough is promised later in the video and is not in this passage.

units.title: Interpret rage clicks as attempts to exit an experience

claim.text: Rage clicks are people clicking multiple times on an element, typically to exit that experience.
claim.quote: this is actually people that you know rage clicking or clicking multiple times on an element typically to kind of exit that experience

args.text: A popup landing in the first few seconds, or a chatbot blocking add-to-cart or form submission, commonly produces rage clicking.
args.quote: you have a popup that lands immediately on the first 5 Seconds somebody's barely even scrolled on the site and they're just rage clicking trying to get rid of that popup

unknowns: The chatbot illustration is given for B2B sites; no general rule is stated.
The source calls rage clicks generally a low hanging fruit opportunity but gives no required value.

units.title: Author's heuristic range for an acceptable rage-click rate

claim.text: The source offers a heuristic that anything under 1 to 2 percent is good.
claim.quote: I would say anything really under 1 to two% is good

unknowns: This is presented as the author's heuristic, not a verified platform benchmark.
The source also describes the observed 0.2% as typically a pretty good rate (0. 2% you know that's typically a pretty good rate), which is not reconciled with the 1 to 2 percent guidance.
The denominator for the rate is not defined in this passage.

units.title: Watch recordings across all insight types regardless of the metric percentage

claim.text: The source says it does not really matter what the metrics are; fundamental usability issues existing on the site should be resolved regardless of the percentage.
claim.quote: it doesn't really matter what the metrics are if there's usability issues fundamental that exist on the site ultimately you want to resolve them regardless of what the percentage is

action.text: Watch the recordings behind all of the insight metrics, not only the ones with high rates.
action.quote: again I would consider watching the recordings of all of these

args.text: An insight metric looks low, for example excessive scrolling under 0.01 percent, and appears not to be a major concern.
args.quote: in this particular scenario it's less than 0.01% so it's not really a major concern

unknowns: The source does not define what counts as a fundamental usability issue or how resolution is verified.

units.title: Understand dead clicks as clicks on elements that are not clickable

claim.text: Dead clicks are when somebody tries to click an element and that element is actually not clickable, hence the word dead.
claim.quote: dead clicks is where somebody tries to click on an element then what happens is that element is actually not clickable hence the word dead

unknowns: No dead-click rate threshold or benchmark is given in this passage.

units.title: Some dead clicks are acceptable when linking out would cost conversions

claim.text: In some scenarios dead clicks are fine because the site may not want to send people outside.
claim.quote: in some scenarios dead clicks are fine because you might not want to send people outside

args.text: Clickable-looking elements such as as seen on or as featured logos risk sending users off-site.
args.quote: you might not necessarily want to send people outbound and outside of the website because your main goal is ultimately conversions

unknowns: The source frames this as an argument for keeping logos non-clickable, i.e. a judgement call rather than a rule.

units.title: Other dead clicks are harmful when clickable elements would help conversion

claim.text: The other scenario is elements that should be clickable and that help people in their journey to conversion actually being not clickable.
claim.quote: there's the other scenario in which elements that should be clickable and that actually help people in their journey to complete a conversion is is not clickable

unknowns: The source does not state how to decide which elements should be clickable beyond the examples given.

units.title: SaaS client pricing section registered dead clicks

claim.text: In a SaaS client audit, people thought pricing elements were clickable, but the only clickable element was the button for getting a number of free credits.
claim.quote: people thought that these elements were clickable but the only element that was actually clickable was the button that said get X number of free credits

unknowns: Client identity, dates, traffic volume and conversion impact are not stated in this passage.
The source adds that it would benefit users if those elements were clickable because people want the price, but the fix applied is not described.

units.title: Non-clickable site logo produced dead clicks and rage clicks

claim.text: People were clicking the logo in the center of the site and the logo was not clickable.
claim.quote: people were actually clicking on this logo uh in the center of the site and the logo wasn't even clickable

args.text: The pattern was noticed on the main dashboard and confirmed by watching recordings of people.
args.quote: they were kind of Rage clicking and basically going through that dead click where it increased that percentage substantially and we noticed that on the main dashboard and we actually saw recordings of people as well

unknowns: The source states the convention that clicking a logo returns you to the homepage, but does not say whether the logo was made clickable or what effect that had.
Users were trying to reach the homepage from the checkout and product pages; the pages involved are given only in general terms.

units.title: Read excessive scrolling as the user failing to find information

claim.text: Excessive scrolling can mean the user is trying to find information on the site but cannot find it.
claim.quote: it could be the fact that they're the user is trying to find information on the site but they can't find it

args.text: Excessive scrolling is recorded when a visitor scrolls a page top to bottom very quickly.
args.quote: excessive scrolling is when somebody is on a website and they're just scrolling very excessively on a particular page right so that just means they're going from top to bottom like very quickly

unknowns: Candidate causes given by the source are users hunting for reviews, hunting for a missing call to action or price, or skimming a long block of text; no rule for distinguishing them is stated.
The source notes its own example account sat under 0.01 percent for excessive scrolling.

units.title: Read quick backs as information not found immediately

claim.text: With quick backs, people look for information on a page but are not able to find it immediately and bounce back and forth.
claim.quote: people are looking for information on a page but they're not able to find it immediately right so they have to constantly bounce back and forth

args.text: Quick backs are recorded when a visitor goes to a page and quickly returns to the previous one.
args.quote: quick back so this is people where they're going to a page as cler saying right here and then they're quickly returning back to the previous one

unknowns: The only illustration given is a product page expected to show certain information; no benchmark is provided.

units.title: Avoid spending time on dashboard metrics Google Analytics already covers

claim.text: The source says it would really spend too much time there, in the context of funnel, channel, campaign, browser, device and popular-page data that Google Analytics can do as well or better.
claim.quote: so I would really spend too much time there

args.text: Dashboard sections such as smart events, referrer and channel breakdown, campaign source, browser and device data and most popular pages are available in Google Analytics.
args.quote: you can do all of this inside of Google analytics and a much better job at that as well

unknowns: The clause appears garbled, plausibly missing a negation such as wouldn't; its polarity is unresolved and must not be settled from memory.
The list of duplicative metrics is enumerated only loosely across the preceding sentences.

units.title: Open the heat map tab and pick a popular page to review

claim.text: The source says clicking the heat map tab presents the most popular pages of the account.
claim.quote: I'll click on the heat map tab up there and then I'll be presented with the most popular Pages

action.text: Open the heat map tab and click into one of the listed popular pages to review its heat map.
action.quote: let's just click on the homepage here

unknowns: The source says accounts typically list 5 to 10 most popular pages segmented by traffic volume, while the demo account showed only two pages.
How a page is selected for review beyond picking from the list is not stated.

claim.text: The source begins to say the heat map screenshot might not look exactly like what was anticipated for clients whose sites have pop-ups, but the sentence is cut off.
claim.quote: you might have a screenshot here that might not look exactly like what you anticipated for some of our clients where they have pop-ups under website

unknowns: The passage ends mid-phrase after pop-ups under website, so the rest of the pop-up effect and any remedy are missing.
